forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news.title: ‘This is the dream job’: Labour’s Bev Craig on the battle to be Greater Manchester mayor
news.summary:
Polling puts close Burnham ally in lead as she aims to defeat Reform and draw back support from revitalised Greens

Bev Craig was mid-squat at the gym when she was recognised for the first time as the prospective heir to Andy Burnham’s throne. Until recently, the Manchester city council leader could happily have gone about her workout in peace.

But all that changed when Burnham, who DJ’ed at her 40th birthday party last year, won the Makerfield byelection and set up another big electoral contest on his way to becoming prime minister.

news_drafts.headline: Manchester asks government to write off 90% of its high needs deficit, with a decision due in October
news_drafts.lead:
Manchester City Council has applied to the Department for Education to write off 90% of its deficit on high needs, the part of school funding that pays for children with special educational needs and disabilities (the "High Needs Block"). The council's Audit Committee was told on 28 July that the decision was expected in October 2026.

Minutes of that meeting record that the application "was expected in October 2026 and was currently being funded by the Council". Until the department rules, the council is paying for the gap itself. The minutes as summarised here give no figure for the deficit.

The committee meets again on 13 October, within the month in which the decision was expected.

news_drafts.headline: Manchester forecasts £7.7m adult social care overspend after Care Closer to Home programme produced inconclusive benefit modelling
news_drafts.lead: Manchester Council is forecasting an overspend of £7.7m in adult social care by the end of the financial year, after a planned transformation programme failed to deliver expected savings. The council had budgeted for £2.5m in savings from a scheme called Care Closer to Home, which was meant to reduce costs, but the transformation has produced what the council's papers describe as "inconclusive benefit modelling"—meaning the savings cannot be measured or relied upon. The shortfall is driven by rising demand: the council is supporting 36 more people with complex learning disabilities than budgeted, 25 more in supported accommodation, and 44 additional mental health care packages. The papers note that unless the council finds new ways to cut costs or improve efficiency in-year, any further demand growth will push the overspend higher still.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Treasury Management Q2 report 2026-27
findings.headline: PWLB rates April-September 2026 ranged from 4.94% to 6.90% across maturity tenors with 61-62 basis point spreads between quarterly lows and highs
findings.detail: The paper presents PWLB Standard Borrowing Rates for Q1 and Q2 2026-27 across five maturity periods. Quarterly lows were achieved in April for most tenors (e.g. 6.29% on 25-year, 5.70% on 10-year), with 1-year reaching its low of 4.94% in July. Quarterly highs were recorded in mid-September across all tenors (6.90% on 25-year, 6.41% on 10-year, 5.55% on 1-year). The spreads between quarterly lows and highs ranged from 61 to 62 basis points.
findings.matters: The rate environment during the period determines financing costs for borrowing and refinancing decisions; finance directors assess PWLB movement to time debt issuance; lenders evaluate the cost of council debt and market conditions.
findings.quote: The spread shown between the highs and lows for loans of each period in the table above highlight the challenges of the current market environment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 for Treasury Management Q2 report 2026-27
findings.headline: Short and medium-term borrowing continues to offer better value than longer-term borrowing
findings.detail: The advisors' guidance to councils is that shorter-dated borrowing provides better value than locking in longer-term rates at current elevated levels. This reflects the shape of the PWLB curve forecast, where spreads between short and long maturities are material.
findings.matters: Strategic guidance on borrowing maturity profile; with the rate curve elevated, borrowing short-dated and refinancing can reduce total borrowing cost compared to locking in longer-term rates
findings.figures: 5yr PWLB Dec 26: 5.60% vs 50yr: 6.10% (50bp spread). Curve steepens at longer end.
findings.quote: Short and medium-term borrowing continues to offer better value than longer-term borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 for Treasury Management Q2 report 2026-27
findings.headline: Economic upside risks from energy prices and persistent inflation; downside risks from weak demand and softer labour market
findings.detail: The advisors identify principal upside risks as renewed energy-price pressures, more persistent domestic inflation, and a higher market-implied Bank Rate path, driven partly by Middle East conflict affecting oil. Downside risks include weaker demand, softer labour market conditions, and faster reduction in underlying inflation. These risks could move interest rates either direction from forecast.
findings.matters: Forecast accuracy depends on economic stability; identified risks show where outcomes could diverge materially from plan, requiring contingency provisions
findings.figures: CPI currently 3.1%, forecast above 4% in early 2027. Oil price $99pb currently (previously reached $108pb). Forecast utility cost increases: electricity 22%, gas 35%, petrol/diesel 32% by Jan-April 2027.
findings.quote: The principal upside risks are renewed energy-price pressures, more persistent domestic inflation and a higher market-implied path for Bank Rate. Downside risks include weaker demand, softer labour-market conditions and a faster reduction in underlying inflation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 for Treasury Management Q2 report 2026-27
findings.headline: Bank Rate forecast expected to reach 4.0% in Q4 2026 then fall, diverging from market expectation of 4.75% mid-2027 peak
findings.detail: Council treasury advisors forecast Bank Rate will increase to 4.0% in Q4 2026, most likely on 5 November, then fall during H2 2027 as inflation moderates and economic weakness allows monetary loosening. This diverges from market expectations, which price Bank Rate peaking at 4.75% in mid-2027, representing a lower and earlier peak in the advisory's view.
findings.matters: Advisors' forecasts diverging from market expectations signal material assumption differences that affect borrowing costs, refinancing decisions, and economic outlook planning
findings.figures: MUFG forecast: Dec 26 4.0%, Mar 27 4.0%, Sep 27 3.75%, Dec 27 3.50%; Market expectation: 4.75% peak mid-2027
findings.quote: Please note, this is not in line with current market forecasts that suggest Bank Rate will peak at 4.75% mid-2027.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 for Treasury Management Q2 report 2026-27
findings.headline: Investment income forecast increased to 4.0% for H2 2026/27 and 3.65% for 2027/28
findings.detail: The council's treasury advisors have revised upward their forecasts for earnings on council cash investments. The H2 2026/27 rate is now 4.0%, and the 2027/28 rate is 3.65%, improving council income expectations for both the current and next financial year.
findings.matters: Investment income helps offset budget pressures and fund strategic priorities; upward revisions improve the council's financial position
findings.quote: H2 2026/27 investment earnings forecast increased to 4.0%. 2027/28 investment earnings forecast increased to 3.65%.
